title: Does no one else think this is unfair to programmers?
author: DD_Games233
selftext:
I've been reading a ton of posts lately, and I've noticed the general vibe across most communities is that people can't stand AI art, but nobody really cares about AI code.

For example, r/indiegames pretty much outright bans posts about games with AI-generated art, and a lot of YouTubers flat out won't cover games that use AI art. Even Steam's AI disclosure only asks you to disclose AI use in content players directly see, which means AI-written code doesn't need to be disclosed at all.

So you end up with this situation:

Someone who can do art but can't code at all can use AI to make a complete game, and nobody hates on them for it.

Someone who can code but can't do art at all can also use AI to make a complete game, but people will hate on them for it.

So subconsciously, do people think code just isn't worth as much as art when it comes to training data for AI models?

AI only got good at coding because it was fed code written by tons of programmers too.

This kind of unfairness basically feels like saying programmers are lesser than everyone else.

I honestly think this is completely unfair. It's a mass double standard.

Sure, to some extent you could say just let players decide. If your game is good all around, players will make their own choice. But like I said, there are these really unfair rules standing in the way first.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
Coding is definitely an art. The problem is that people have a real hierarchy in their mind for art, and visual art is at the top of that hierarchy. 

  
Coding is also one of those arts that is invisible, unfortunately. And it is not only easier to automate than visual art (right now) but easier to obfuscate the harm done by said automation.

So, yes, it is incredibly unfair.

  
But... there's just little sense, IMHO, in pointing it out. Asymmetry is a constant. It's not fair that I get to live in the magical kingdom making a video game while people in Rwanda hike to get potable water. That sucks ass. We should work to change that and find ways to make the world better. 'Hey, this is unfair!' is a true statement that by itself doesn't move any needles. 

Coding is almost certainly a dead career now. People will probably still code, but increasingly anyone with commercial goals will automate it. If you were looking forward to a coding career, I am genuinely sorry; your best approach is to swallow the very bitter medicine and try to find an alternative career where you can transfer your skills.

replies.author: DD_Games233
replies.body: I'm speaking up because I just hope players can be a bit more understanding toward indie devs like me who don't have art skills. If someone leaves a negative review because my game looks rough overall or just isn't fun, I'll take that on board. But if someone writes it off purely because it uses AI art, with no other reason at all, that's kind of hard for me to accept.

comments.author: earlvanze
comments.body:
Not at all unfair, we just move up the value chain and abstraction layers.

Is it unfair that we're not programming games on low-level ROMs anymore?

Abstraction just goes onto higher layers. Programmers understand this the most.

replies.author: DD_Games233
replies.body: I agree that AI lets programmers work at a higher level. My question is why the same reasoning isn’t applied to artists or the other people using AI.

comments.author: Live_Meeting_1121
comments.body:
As a programmer I don't care. Code was always cheap and easy to do, the real work is building systems and architecture. I have seen the vibe coded projects from my artists friends, it's a mess but they are happy it works, so I'm happy they are happy.

We just exchange our worries and tell them where the pitfalls are, the issue comes mostly when they have been too deep in the code rabbit hole, it's hard to roll back to something more maintenable.

From the perspective of someone vibecoding what they are mostly losing is money on context overload.

From the perspective of a programmer, what I see they are losing isn't only that but much more.

But in the same way my understanding of certain things is limited by my knowledge and practices, so is theirs.

So the point is, do whatever, but if you don't collaborate you might go blind into fields of knowledge you dont properly understand. So, collaborate, ask for help, learn.

replies.author: DD_Games233
replies.body: I’m happy your artist friends can use AI to make working games. That’s exactly the acceptance I’m asking for in the other direction: programmers using AI art to make their games. My concern isn’t code quality or being replaced—it’s why one is accepted while the other is condemned.

replies.author: Vindelator
replies.body:
(This isn't quite my view on things, but this seems to be why people hate AI art.)  
  
Art is supposed to be a reflection of our humanity.

It's the exact short of thing that should be separating people from machines. Our creativity and our ability to think abstractly. 

So people see AI as some kinda attack on what makes us human. 

**This is way too limited a perspective though.** It's the sort of thing people who don't make art or code might think.

For me, I don't like shitty things. If the AI art looks good, then it's good.  
  
I don't care of SandTextureNumber43.jpg was made with computers using ai or make with computers using photoshop. 

I've seen people make generic slop and I've seen creative things done with AI.

comments.author: xavium
comments.body:
Welcome to game dev lol. I feel games are art, but the visual side is all people see. They rarely understand the technical expertise needed behind making a game feel good and the mechanics, engine, physics, particle effects, post process, shaders, etc. 
People also generally just expect all that stuff to work. And only when it doesn't is it the programmers' faults. Found a funny bug? Haha programmers dumb and didn't make the game good enough. 
My experience has taught me that the best game programmers go unnoticed, if everything works as it should, or better even, and nobody says "why did it do that" then you did a good job. 
Like a movie, nobody really thinks about the people who make the cameras that it's filmed on. 

In regards to AI being involved in this, it's a tool, or an evolution of the way of developing. Before assembly came around, and then high-level languages, there were people who only knew machine code and had great skill at understanding it. That knowledge became obsolete and even assembly is not strictly necessary to know anymore. The issue is that AI is as capable as it is because it was given everything, so there's a yucky feeling if you think about people's expertise being used to further the tech without them being credited or paid for it. Or even asked beforehand. 

It'll go away in time as we lean more on AI as a society and for more technology. I feel like the majority just wish it wasn't a thing, and by not supporting it they can keep the status quo for a while longer.

comments.author: UsherOfDestruction
comments.body:
I'm with you. It's completely hypocritical. Don't you dare devalue what artists do. Software developers? Fuck 'em. We can all do their job now. If you're an artist with no coding experience vibe developing games, shame on you. Just because the general public doesn't have our backs the same way it does yours, doesn't mean what you're doing is right. 

I always see people going "But AI art is shitty. It can't do what a human can the same as with code." Fucking nonsense. Hook AI up to Blender or Krita through MCP and give it very explicit instructions, it can produce high quality art. If you just go to ChatGPT and tell imagegen "Make a photorealistic cat and animate it" then yeah, you're gonna get whatever trash it can throw at you. The art isn't in the hand that's drawing, it's in the mind that's imagining. Artists just practiced, trained and know how to translate that to physical mediums. Just like I practiced, trained and know how to translate my imaginings into code. 

But then people will throw art into diagnosis tools which tell them it's AI and they have a fucking meltdown. Please. 

I think some of it is just vengeful thinking. Artists have long been shit on. No doubt about it. I've bought so much of my friends art over my life. Shit I didn't care a bit about but recognized the quality and felt they should be supported so they could make even more art to reach the people who do care about their artform. And on some level people still think of software engineers as overpaid brats who get to sit and play on a computer all day. People in my life have seen me struggle with problems, have anxiety over what I'm producing and be mentally fucking exhausted at the end of many days and unable to do anything but just mindlessly veg out. And I'd still get comments about how my job was easy and just fun compared to theirs. I think both of those contribute to the protect artists but fuck software developers mindset.

comments.author: Maximum-Touch-9294
comments.body:
Because some of the loudest people complaining about AI art seem determined to hate anything with an AI label attached to it.

Remember that experiment where a guy posted an actual Monet painting, claimed it was AI-generated in the style of Monet, and asked people to explain why it was inferior to the real thing?

All these self-proclaimed art experts came out explaining how it had no soul, lacked emotion, and looked nothing like a real Monet.

Except it WAS a real Monet. 😂

That experiment exposed something hilarious: some people aren't judging the art at all. They're judging what they think created it.

And the irony is that a blank white canvas can be praised as a profound artistic statement, but suddenly a beautiful image has "no soul" the moment someone believes AI made it.

Maybe we should judge creative work by its actual quality instead of obsessing over which tools were used to create it.

comments.author: AltruisticPossible84
comments.body:
People look at art as an extension of human creativity that has been with us since before we could speak or write. It's seen as an intrinsic part of the human experience that is inseparable from consciousness and creativity 

Computer programming, altho it can be a creative pursuit, is seen foremost as a means to an end. It's necessary to get these dang computers to work. Computers that are, by definition, not part of our natural world. Therefore, programming is an industrial process, first. It's more science than art.

  
Having AI do art for you is potentially undermining your humanity, while coding a project is just lazy but unoffensive to the person consuming the end product.
